# Discussion

Attack in a 30 m cell was predicted first by attack in and around it the year before, the order @aukema2008 followed on the Chilcotin Plateau, where temperature still "contributed to explaining outbreak probabilities" once neighbouring and earlier outbreaks were in the model (p. 348). The best neighbourhood here was `r A_NB` m, close to the 140 m within which previous attack raised red attack above its background in Colorado [@walter2013], and the outbreak was in the phase in which "almost all new mortality was associated with intensification of existing outbreaks, not expansion" [@meddens2014, p. 83]. The three refugia mechanisms that @krawchuk2020 proposed were therefore tested as modifiers of an outbreak that spread mostly by contagion, and the novelty of the study lay in testing the three together on one landscape at 30 m with that dependence in the model, which few earlier studies had done. Density and shade by terrain moved as the hypothesis predicted and host size did not, wind lowered attack only in open stands and only over sixteen-day periods, and ground facing the afternoon wind had the least attack.

## Refugia mechanisms

Beside contagion, attack rose with the amount of host, the basis of the stand susceptibility rating used in British Columbia, which is built on "the percentage of susceptible pine by basal area", pine age and stand density [@safranyik2010, p. 429; @shore2000susceptibility], so the refugia this landscape showed were thin stands with little pine, as in thinning trials in which stands reduced in basal area lost fewer trees [@mitchell1983thinning; @fettig2007effectiveness; @hood2016fortifying]. The amount of host is itself a product of forest history, because within climatically suitable areas "forest age-class structure will be the primary factor influencing host susceptibility and outbreak severity" [@taylor2003, p. 42]. Live stems ran the other way because a stand of many stems was a crowded stand, in which trees grow slowly and have thin phloem [@shore2006], so the count of stems measured the size of the trees more than the amount of host.

Shade by terrain protected ground once attack nearby was in the model, through the sky view and the sun of the flight window, which was the mechanism @krawchuk2020 proposed, cooler ground that protects trees from water stress, although the effect was lost under the spatial field and at a 270 m grain, so it was a property of the slope at the scale of a stand and not of the landscape. The faces that were cooler by aspect did not share it. North-facing ground had more attack, the reverse of the Morice Timber Supply Area, where the most intense infestations were found early on warmer slopes facing south and west [@nelson2007environmental], although its surface was `r num(STSM$st_south_mean - STSM$st_north_mean, "%.1f")` °C cooler in the late morning. Two observations of the beetle's flight point to heat during flight rather than water stress. The heaviest attacks on a bole are "usually found on the northern aspect" [@safranyik2006chap1, p. 18], and in the Black Hills "The decreased number of attacks during midday coincides with the period of highest mean temperatures" [@schmid1991bark, p. 1445], so the sunlit afternoon faces may have been too hot for landing beetles while the ground shaded by terrain was too cool for the brood, where summers too cool for development in one year make mass attack less successful [@safranyik2006chap1; @logan2001].

Attack peaked in stands of 25 to 30 cm quadratic mean diameter, just above the 25 cm at which lodgepole pines change on average from beetle sinks to beetle sources [@carroll2004bionomics], because thicker phloem feeds more brood, from an average of 16 beetles to 94 as phloem thickened from 2.3 to 5.8 mm [@amman1972]. Attack fell in stands of larger trees because those stands held little pine, not because the beetle avoided large trees [@shore2006], and epidemics also "often deplete the large diameter pine component of stands" [@shore2006, p. 110]. The scarcity of large trees therefore made a refugium only below 25 cm, where the trees could not feed a brood, and above 30 cm the refugium was the absence of pine. Elevation had the largest coefficient in every model, against the historical decline of mortality with elevation [@shore2006], but on this range the higher ground also held the pine, as in western Montana [@wulder2006red], and milder winters after 1976 had favoured outbreaks at height [@maciasfauria2009].

## Wind and openness

Wind lowered attack where the canopy was open and raised it where the canopy was closed, so the stand property through which wind acted was crown closure. That was the mechanism @bartos1989 proposed in the Uinta Mountains of Utah, where a thinned stand was windier than the unthinned stand beside it by 3.2 km/h or more in the late afternoon and, in a recently thinned stand, "canopy density usually is insufficient to trap the pheromone and move it horizontally to attract other beetles" (p. 9), and a tracer gas released in place of pheromone was diluted fastest in the most open of three canopies [@thistle2004surrogate]. The effect appeared with the terrain wind over sixteen-day periods and not with the station wind interpolated from the valleys, which varied between periods and years but hardly between cells, so the test needed a wind that differed from one slope to the next within a season. In the annual models wind raised attack everywhere, more so where basal area was greater. Wind above the canopy carries beetles into new stands [@jackson2008; @chen2017], which predicts more attack with wind where large hosts stand under a closed canopy, and under epidemic pressure pheromones from attacked trees nearby "may override the positive benefits of increased spacing and improved tree growth derived from partial cutting" [@schmid2005, p. 9]. For management the two readings agree, since a stand opened by thinning was protected by the wind only during flight and least where attacked trees stood close.

## Shelter and deposition

The afternoon air reached the site from the south-west, from `r pv(TRB[1])` to `r pv(TRB[2])` degrees, and the least attack fell on the faces that met it, `r fpa("south")` per cent of cells on south-facing and `r fpa("south-west")` per cent on south-west-facing ground against `r fpa("west")` per cent on west-facing and `r fpa("north-west")` per cent on north-west-facing ground. This was the reverse of most studies of aspect, in which attack favoured southern slopes [@walter2013; @nelson2007environmental], and of the Peace River region, where beetles "tend to accumulate on windward sides of barriers" [@giroday2011, p. 1107]. Beetles released by @safranyik1989 "climbed towards the tree tops, and usually tracked to the north or northeast, generally crosswind and downwind" (p. 508), and "bark beetles do not fly in winds that exceed their maximum flight speed" [@carroll2004bionomics, pp. 22-23]. These observations suggest that the afternoon wind lifted beetles up the south and south-west faces, carried them over the ridges and set them down on the north and west faces beyond, where the wind slackened. That would explain the least attack on the windward faces, the fall in attack where the wind was pushed up the slope, steepest on ridges and spurs, and a shelter effect that did not depend on the stand, as deposition predicted and plume disruption did not, and it matches the reading @kunegel2020factors gave of a north-facing onset in the Cypress Hills, where "the dominant winds in Cypress Hills come from the south-west" (p. 9). Deposition also depends on the stand, since in simulations of beetles flying through forest, dispersal downwind shortened as trunks became denser [@byers2000]. The shelter index taken at one fixed bearing was small, was lost at a 90 m grain and changed sign under the spatial field, so it described where attack clustered as much as a property of the slope, and a refugium defined at 30 m and one defined at 1 km were different things, the concern for scale that @aukema2008 raised. No study had compared beetles landing on the windward and lee faces of the same ridge, and the test of this hypothesis would be a record of wind and of landing beetles on the slopes themselves.

## Limits and management

The response was classified rather than observed, and the classifier's accuracy measured its separation of the field plots from undisturbed forest rather than agreement with ground mortality across the landscape [@meddens2013]. The inventory postdated part of the outbreak, the terrain wind took its direction from the reanalysis and gave about half the speed measured on the valley floor, and the study covered one mountain range over `r spellnum(nrow(ARS))` outbreak years. For management, the refugia this landscape showed were stands with little host, the structure that thinning and a younger age structure produce, which terrain maps alone could not locate. Partial cutting substantially lowers the susceptibility of lodgepole pine stands [@mata2003; @shore2000susceptibility], but in ponderosa pine it "may be ineffective for partially cut parcels of \<10 acres if the partially cut stands are surrounded by unmanaged susceptible stands" [@schmid2005], which the dominance of attack nearby supported, and @six2014management found the field evidence that thinning protects stands during an outbreak weaker than policy had assumed.
